title: Anya Taylor-Joy's 'Lucky' Divides Critics with Mixed Reviews Amidst Star-Studded Promotion
text:
Apple TV+'s new series Lucky, starring and co-produced by Anya Taylor-Joy, has sparked a range of critical reactions following its premiere. While some reviewers praise Taylor-Joy's performance and the show's pace, others denounce it as formulaic and better suited as a film.
Anya Taylor-Joy was seen leaving the SiriusXM Studios in New York City on Wednesday, where she had been promoting her new Apple TV+ series Lucky, which she co-produced alongside Reese Witherspoon .
Dressed in a flowing green maxi dress detailed with white lace at the neckline, paired with white strappy heels and silver jewelry, the actress presented an ethereal image as she stepped out in the Big Apple following an interview with radio host Andy Cohen. Lucky, which premiered on Apple TV+ on July 15, has attracted a spectrum of critical reactions since the release of its first two episodes, ranging from praise for Taylor-Joy's performance to harsh condemnation of the show's formulaic storytelling.
The series, directed by Jet Wilkinson, centers on Taylor-Joy's character, con artist Luciana 'Lucky' Armstrong, who is compelled to flee after a major heist goes awry. Pursued by both the FBI and a formidable crime boss portrayed by Annette Bening, Lucky's journey forms the core of this seven-part thriller. Early reviews have highlighted a stark divide in opinion.
The Daily Telegraph delivered a scathing two-star assessment, with critic Ed Power dismissing the adaptation as unoriginal and cliché-ridden, likening it to a 'mash-up of Pulp Fiction and one of those Nineties Leonard adaptations.
' Power argued that despite Taylor-Joy's star power, the character is predominantly defined by the men around her and that the actress appears 'mildly discommoded' throughout, contrasting with Timothy Olyphant's apparently more enjoyable, self-aware performance. A similarly critical two-star review on Roger Ebert's site, penned by Brian Tallerico, framed Lucky as a prime example of streaming television's 'Why Isn't This a Movie' problem, suggesting the narrative would have been more effective as a compact, two-hour film rather than a padded seven-episode series.
Tallerico noted that with only about 10-15 minutes of substantial plot per 45-minute episode, the show often feels like a wasted opportunity to deliver a lean thriller. The Guardian offered a middling three-star review, acknowledging the show's flaws-including a weak script and an unusual theme song by Fiona Apple-but ultimately categorizing it as passable 'classic summer viewing.
' The review whimsically suggests that during the summer months, when energy wanes, viewers might 'raise our Slush Puppie to the good bits' such as performances by Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor and Annette Bening, while choosing to 'quietly flee through the nearest window from the rest. ' In contrast, The Wrap praised the series as a 'non-stop thrills show' with a fast pace that introduces new complications regularly, building momentum throughout.
This divergence in critical opinion underscores the ongoing debate about the series' quality and whether its extended format serves or hinders its suspenseful premise
